messages.subject: Default Number of Quadrature Points for MultipleGroup Function
messages.subject_clean: Default Number of Quadrature Points for MultipleGroup Function
messages.body_plain:
Good Evening, Dr. Chalmers,

I am using the MultipleGroup function in the MIRT package to test for DIF using a unidimensional scale. If quadpts = 'Null', what is the number of quadrature points used?

Thanks in advance,
Quintin
messages.body_snippet:

messages.body_plain:
Hi Quintin,

The default for unidimensional models is to use 41. Most of the details in the estimation can be found in the ?mirt help file (this goes for mirt(), mixedmirt(), bfactor(), and multipleGroup() too). Cheers.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: How many items are needed to calculate M2 Statistic?
messages.subject_clean: How many items are needed to calculate M2 Statistic?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,

I want to know a one more thing.

What kind can I try special optimizers?

2014년 6월 19일 목요일 오전 4시 34분 34초 UTC+9, Phil Chalmers 님의 말:

> On Wed, Jun 18, 2014 at 3:30 PM, Seongho Bae <seongh...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Okay, I will check out your advice soon. :)
> >
> > Anyway, If I can't know to get a rule of thumb for IRT models from many complex reasons, May I get CFI, TLI, and RMSEA using alternative methods without calculation of M2 statistic in the graded response model?
>
> Not that I'm aware of. Your only other bet for these types of models is to compare them with structural equation modeling methods using special optimizers (like the WLSMV). But even then, I'm not sure how well those are standardized compared to using continuous data, were they were initially studied in depth.
>
> Phil
>
> >
> > 2014년 6월 19일 목요일 오전 3시 58분 42초 UTC+9, Phil Chalmers 님의 말:
> > > It's pretty difficult to give a rule of thumb for IRT models since it depends on many things, including, but not limited to: item skewness, dimensionality, item type, parameter type (slopes are generally harder to estimate than intercepts), etc. Also whether your end goal is to ultimately create reasonable predictions of θ will matter, since estimating too many imprecise item level parameters will cause imprecision in these predictions (the so-called parameter drift issue) but including too few item parameters may give larger SE's than you'd like to tolerate.
> > >
> > > Might be better to refer to simulation studies like the following to get a better idea of these models:
> > >
> > > Forero, C. G. & Maydeu-Olivares, A. Estimation of IRT Graded Response Models: Limited Versus Full Information Methods. Psychological Methods, 2009, 14, 275-299.
> > >
> > >
> > > On Wed, Jun 18, 2014 at 12:20 PM, Seongho Bae <seongh...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > I collapsing six categories to four categories. That's so helpful advice in my case. When I had six categories, I can't get a clear item trace lines. But after collapsing four categories, I can get, the more clear item trace lines.
> > > >
> > > > Anyway, How many samples are needed for estimating 6 intercepts per item? I want to know it's practical issues.
> > > >
> > > > 2014년 6월 19일 목요일 오전 12시 58분 22초 UTC+9, Phil Chalmers 님의 말:
> > > > > You can do this of course, but you'll lose the property of you test being polytomous and ordered (and as a consequence lose precision when trying to estimate θ, if that's your end goal). How you try and dichotomize the data will also affect the fit statistics as well as the estimated parameters, so it's not entirely clear what the best way to dichotomize is. I would recommend trying to preserve the nature of your test to the best of your ability, since in the end that's likely what you are trying to understand. Collapsing from 7 to 5 categories isn't unheard of in the literature, but reviewers may have a bigger issue when going from 7 to only 2. Cheers.
> > > > >
> > > > > Phil
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Wed, Jun 18, 2014 at 11:54 AM, Seongho Bae <seongh...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > Thanks for your advice, Dr Phil. ;)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Your main advices were collapsing the first category into second, and the last category into second last. So, I have a one more question. Can I convert this item responses to dichotomous type to save degree of freedom?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Seongho Bae.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 2014년 6월 19일 목요일 오전 12시 48분 39초 UTC+9, Phil Chalmers 님의 말:
> > > > > > > There are 78 unique first and second moments which are used in computing the M2* statistic, 12 * (12 + 1)/2. However, if you fit these data with the graded model, each item has 7 parameters estimated (1 slope and 6 intercepts). That makes 7 * 12 = 84 parameters, so you're just shy of having a meaningful statistic, and is why there is not enough df. This is one of the issues with the M2* statistic.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > You could try collapsing one or more categories in your data to try and compute the M2. If you collapse say the last category into the second last, and the first category into the second, then that will save you 24 df and you'll be able to calculate the M2 statistic properly with good room for variation (though of course that is a slightly different model, but in your case since the sample size is so small estimating 6 intercepts per item is probably way too much anyway). Hope that helps.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Wed, Jun 18, 2014 at 11:36 AM, Seongho Bae <seongh...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > > > > > >

Okay, I see the issue now. The problem doesn't actually have to do with M2() but rather happens when the statistical null model (the model in which all slopes are constrained to be 0) is computed and a type of 'divide-by-zero' issue is happening in the E-step causing NaN's to pop up where they shouldn't. I've made a patch for this on the dev version.

The following code will crash with versions less than 1.4.2 for numerical reasons, but will run on the dev now and therefore should fix your problem.

# Calc null model manually
sv <- mirt(dat, 1, pars = 'values')
sv$value[sv$name == 'a1'] <- 0
sv$est[sv$name == 'a1'] <- FALSE
null.model <- mirt(dat, 1, pars=sv)

Cheers.

messages.body_plain:
The impute options are used to obtain plausible values of what the missing data would look like given a θ input, and the variability is collected using traditional multiple imputation methods. We do this so that we have full datasets to work with, even though they are only instantaneous stand-ins.

So, the number of draws required should be somewhat proportional to the amount of missingness observed. In the examples, 10 was used as just an example, but probably more than 100 or more should be used if missingness occurs a lot. That way variability of the missingness will be better captured in the statistics.

Phil

Hi Phil,

I have a question on mixedmirt() function. Based on the function description and examples that you have provided, I understand that person-level and item-level covariate terms can be entered into a mirt model, using the 'covdata' and 'itemdesign' dataframes, respectively. An application of this kind of specification is in performing a confirmatory MIRT modeling of data, where certain items are found to illustrate differential item functioning for some subject groups (such as gender or race). The covariate-item interaction terms will then basically measure difference in item difficulties between patient groups (in case of uniform DIF).

I am aware that parameter estimation in this scenario can be performed using the 'multipleGroup' function. However, I am trying to use mirt package for a problem that involves longitudinal modeling of subjects' responses, which will require use of random covariate terms, as in 'mixedmirt' function.

I would appreciate your help in this regard.

Thanks,
Nishant

Hi Nishant,

This is an interesting question, but I'm having trouble understanding what it would look like. Usually when you include person-level covariates these effects are in some way time invariant and therefore should affect all item responses (hence, form the regression θ = β X + ε, where θ is simply being modeled by other relevant fixed factors). So its difficult for me to understand why some person-level covariates would be non-existent across items. Could you perhaps provide an example of this?

I think the interpretation of item blocks interacting with person level covariates makes sense for the most part, where, say, the first n items form block 1, while the next k form block 2, then the interaction of person level covariates with block design (or individual items, if you go that way to form as many blocks as items) would signify how the items modulate the person level variables across the item design blocks....but this would 'remove' them per say, just modify their influence for different blocks and require an extra coefficient to be estimated. However, I think this is probably the effect you are going for anyway. Hope that helps.

Phil

Hi Phil,

Thanks for your reply. Yes, you are correct that if there are person-level covariates that affect the underlying latent traits (θ), then all items should illustrate the effects of these covariate terms. However, I was trying to point towards a slightly different scenario wherein, the covariate terms actually affect the item characteristic curves of certain items rather than the latent traits. I am not sure if statistical modeling theory has been developed for such scenarios. As an example, let us consider a test designed for measuring memory recall in subjects. Now, certain items on the test turn out to be biased because subjects belonging to a particular occupation are exposed to similar contents (as in the biased items) in everyday life and, therefore, they illustrate much higher likelihood of responding to those items correctly. During IRT modeling, this effect can be easily detected using DIF and, traditionally, such items may be removed from the test. If item deletion is not an option (such as in the case of retrospective analysis of tests that were not analyzed with IRT during design), separate IRT modeling of subject groups can also be performed. However, this would result in different item and subject scales. Therefore, it would be quite meaningful to have a methodology to be able to incorporate DIF effects within the model so that all subjects are measured on the same scale. For example, if DIF is uniform in nature, then the item response function (IRF) can contain a fixed intercept effect to adjust the difficulty parameter for certain subject groups. In mathematical terms, this model will look as containing person-covariate terms in IRFs of only some items in the test. Such covariate terms will basically account for changes in IRF functions due to DIF across subject groups. However, if there are person-level covariate terms across all items in the test, that will account for factors that may affect the underlying latent traits - thereby, affecting all items in the test. Does this make any sense ?

Thanks,
Nishant

On Thu, Jul 31, 2014 at 11:04 AM, Nishant Verma <nisha...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Phil,

> Thanks for your reply. Yes, you are correct that if there are person-level covariates that affect the underlying latent traits (θ), then all items should illustrate the effects of these covariate terms. However, I was trying to point towards a slightly different scenario wherein, the covariate terms actually affect the item characteristic curves of certain items rather than the latent traits. I am not sure if statistical modeling theory has been developed for such scenarios. As an example, let us consider a test designed for measuring memory recall in subjects. Now, certain items on the test turn out to be biased because subjects belonging to a particular occupation are exposed to similar contents (as in the biased items) in everyday life and, therefore, they illustrate much higher likelihood of responding to those items correctly. During IRT modeling, this effect can be easily detected using DIF and, traditionally, such items may be removed from the test. If item deletion is not an option (such as in the case of retrospective analysis of tests that were not analyzed with IRT during design), separate IRT modeling of subject groups can also be performed. However, this would result in different item and subject scales. Therefore, it would be quite meaningful to have a methodology to be able to incorporate DIF effects within the model so that all subjects are measured on the same scale. For example, if DIF is uniform in nature, then the item response function (IRF) can contain a fixed intercept effect to adjust the difficulty parameter for certain subject groups.

But this is exactly what an interaction of group membership by item does, create an extra intercept that only affects one group and not the other by design. So in short, yes this is possible to do in mixedmirt(), just specify a design matrix for items which you believe are systematically easier/more difficult given the group membership, and form an interaction term between the two in the model formula. Actually, if your model is a Rasch type this could also be done with lme4, so it might be good to check out the literature on how to do this with generalized mixed effects models as well (at least conceptually it will help).

> In mathematical terms, this model will look as containing person-covariate terms in IRFs of only some items in the test. Such covariate terms will basically account for changes in IRF functions due to DIF across subject groups. However, if there are person-level covariate terms across all items in the test, that will account for factors that may affect the underlying latent traits - thereby, affecting all items in the test. Does this make any sense ?

Yes it does, and it really does sound like a simple uniform DIF test for each item of interest (or modeled all at once). The key is to form the appropriate itemdesign data.frame and have the specific terms interact with the group membership. You'll need a column for each item of interest in the data.frame, but otherwise it should be easy to construct. Cheers.

Phil
